mainTopic: From the תם ox that killed, through whether there is an assessment for damages, to the laws of payment for shame (בושת) in the משנה
overview: The amud opens by finishing a report by רבא. The scholars of בי רב say a תם ox that injured and then killed is judged only for its life, because a money case needs a court evaluation and a death sentence may not wait for one. רבא answers that the ruling could even follow רבי עקיבא, in a case where the owner ran away. The גמרא tests this, and רב מרי concludes that the ox's plowing earnings belong to its owner, so they cannot pay for this damage. Next the גמרא asks whether the court assesses if an act was strong enough to cause damage. Proofs from a pit and from a slave are pushed aside, but a ברייתא of שמעון התימני proves that objects are assessed. The גמרא then works through the משנה about shame. Spit on clothing pays nothing, because shaming with words is exempt. 'Everything follows his honor' is a leniency for the poor, as רבי עקיבא's reply shows. The court may give time to pay for בושת. Finally, רבא resolves a contradiction about hurting oneself, and the challenge to his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The court does not delay a death verdict to evaluate damages
steps.stepSummary: The scholars of בי רב, as reported by רבא, finish their reasoning. Money cases need a court evaluation, and once the ox is sentenced to death we may not hold it back for that evaluation.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we see that we need the court's evaluation. And this ox, once its verdict was given for death, we do not hold it back for the court's evaluation, and we do not delay its judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the explanation of בי רב for why the ברייתא says the ox is judged only for its life and not for the money. They say it is because a money ruling needs a court evaluation, and a death sentence cannot wait for that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא follows the view that a money case needs an אומדנא, a court estimate of the damage, and estimating takes time. A death sentence, once given, must be carried out without delay, so there is no time left for the money case. This means the ברייתא does not follow רבי עקיבא, who needs no such evaluation.

keyTerms.meaning: So we see / apparently (introduces a conclusion)
The court's evaluation (estimate) of the damage
Its verdict was given for death

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the whole debate. בי רב tie the ברייתא to the view that needs a court evaluation, and רבא will try to show it can fit רבי עקיבא too.

phrases.english: Apparently, we require the court's evaluation;
and this one, since its verdict was concluded for death,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the ox that killed.

phrases.aramaic: לָא מְשַׁהֵינַן לֵיהּ לְאוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי דִינָא,
phrases.english: we do not delay it for the court's evaluation,
and we do not delay its judgment.
phrases.notes: Literally 'we do not torment its judgment.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אלמא בעינן אומדנא דבי דינא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the explanation of בי רב, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money damages need a court evaluation, and a death verdict may not be delayed for it, so the money case is never judged.

steps.title: רבא: the case is where the owner ran away
steps.stepSummary: רבא suggests that the ברייתא could follow רבי עקיבא if the owner of the ox ran away, so no money ruling can be made against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And I said to them: Even if you say it follows רבי עקיבא, what case are we dealing with here? A case where the owner ran away.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא tells the scholars of בי רב that their explanation is not the only option. The ברייתא could even follow רבי עקיבא, if the owner ran away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי עקיבא there is no evaluation to wait for, so the reason given by בי רב does not work for him. רבא gives a different reason the money case is not judged: the owner is not there to be ruled against.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (introduces a narrowed case)

phrases.english: And I said to them:
phrases.notes: רבא is now speaking for himself, answering the scholars of בי רב.

phrases.english: Even if you say it follows Rabbi Akiva,
what are we dealing with here?
For instance, where he fled.
phrases.notes: The one who ran away is the owner of the ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: ואמינא להו אנא אפילו תימא רבי עקיבא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different explanation from the one given by בי רב in step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא could only follow the view that needs a court evaluation.
steps.terutzMaskana: It can follow רבי עקיבא too, if the owner ran away.

steps.title: How can the court judge money with the owner gone?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא: if the owner ran away, no money case could be judged at all, so why does the ברייתא imply one is judged when there is no death case?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he ran away, then even where the court did not judge the ox with דיני נפשות, how could it judge it with דיני ממונות without the owner?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's idea. If the owner is gone, the court could never judge the money case, even where there is no death case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא suggests that the only thing blocking the money case is the death case. Under רבא's idea, the owner's absence would block the money case anyway. That makes the death case pointless as the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Capital cases (judging for life or death)

phrases.english: If he fled,
then when they did not judge it with capital law,
how do we judge it with monetary law
without the owner?

steps.triggerLanguage: אי ברח כי לא דנוהו דיני נפשות היכי דיינינן ליה דיני ממונות בלא בעלים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case רבא described in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the owner ran away
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A court cannot judge money against an owner who is absent. So the owner's absence alone would block the money case, and the death case would not be the reason, as the ברייתא suggests.

steps.title: The witnesses testified before he ran
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the court accepted the witnesses' testimony while the owner was there, and only afterwards he ran away.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where the court accepted the witnesses, and then he ran away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא. The testimony was taken while the owner was present, so the court can rule on the money even after he leaves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the witnesses are accepted in the owner's presence, the court may finish the money case without him. So without a death case, the money case could go ahead, and רבא's case stays standing.

keyTerms.meaning: The court accepted the witnesses' testimony

phrases.english: Where [the court] accepted witnesses, and [then] he fled.

steps.triggerLanguage: דקביל סהדי וברח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner was absent the whole time, so no money ruling was ever possible.
steps.terutzMaskana: The testimony was taken while he was present, so a money ruling is possible after he runs.

steps.title: Where does the payment come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: with the owner gone, where will the payment for the damage come from?
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, from where is the damage paid?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about רבא's case. With the owner gone, who actually pays?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the court can issue a ruling, it needs a source of money to collect from. This question prepares the next step, which names that source.

phrases.english: Ultimately, from where is it paid?

steps.triggerLanguage: סוף סוף מהיכא משתלם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Probes further into the case set up in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source of the payment when the owner has run away.

steps.title: Payment comes from the ox's plowing
steps.stepSummary: The damage is paid from the earnings of hiring out the ox to plow.
steps.simpleTranslation: From plowing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ox is hired out to plow, and the earnings pay for the damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court can collect from the ox's work even though the owner is not there. This answer will lead straight into the next challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: Plowing (the ox's earnings from plowing work)

phrases.english: From plowing.
phrases.notes: The ox is hired out to plow fields, and that money goes to the injured side.

steps.triggerLanguage: מרידיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The damage is paid from the earnings of hiring the ox out to plow.

steps.title: Then judge the money case first and the death case after
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if payment can come from plowing, the court should judge the money case first, collect from the plowing, and only then judge the ox for its life.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, with a תם ox, let the court judge the money case first and collect from the plowing, and afterwards judge the death case!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the plowing answer against רבא. If the money can come from plowing, there is no reason to skip the money case. Just do it before the death case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said a תם ox is judged only for its life and not for the money. But if the money can be collected from plowing, the court could handle both cases in order: money first, then life. So רבא's explanation seems not to account for the ruling of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox with no history of goring (pays half damages from its own body)

steps.whatToRemember: רבא tries to fit the ברייתא to רבי עקיבא through a case where the owner ran away. The גמרא pushes back step by step. The witnesses were accepted before he ran, and the payment comes from plowing. That last point raises a new problem: why not judge the money case first and the death case after?

phrases.english: If so, an innocuous ox:
let us judge it with monetary law first,
and it will be paid from plowing,
and then let us judge it with capital law!

steps.triggerLanguage: אי הכי תם נדייניה דיני ממונות ברישא ונשתלם מרידיא והדר נדייניה דיני נפשות
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the plowing answer of step 6 to challenge רבא's explanation in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that the owner ran away, together with the plowing answer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the money can be collected from plowing without the owner, nothing stops the court from judging the money case first and then the death case. That goes against the ברייתא's ruling that a תם ox is judged only for its life.

steps.title: Plowing earnings belong to the owner, not to the ox
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא concludes that money earned from plowing with the ox counts as the owner's general property. That is why it cannot be used to pay for the ox's damage, and why the court does not judge the money case first.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, son of רב כהנא, said: This shows that the earnings from plowing are the superior property of the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי answers the challenge from step 7. He learns from the court's practice that plowing money belongs to the owner, not to the ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 asked why the court does not collect damages from the plowing money first and only then judge the ox for its life. רב מרי says this practice itself teaches a rule: plowing earnings belong to the owner's general property. Payment for this damage comes only from the ox's own value, so the plowing money cannot be used, and there is no reason to judge the money case first.

keyTerms.meaning: "This says": a rule we learn from what was just discussed
Earnings from hiring out the ox to plow

steps.whatToRemember: Money earned by working an animal counts as the owner's property, not as part of the animal's own value.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as saying the plowing money pays the damage. It says the opposite: the money belongs to the owner, so it is not part of the ox that pays for the damage.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא,
phrases.english: Rav Mari, son of Rav Kahana, said:
This says:
phrases.notes: He learns this from the fact that the court doesn't judge the money case first, the problem raised in step 7.

phrases.english: Plowing earnings are the superior property of its owner.
phrases.notes: He means the plowing money counts as the owner's own property, not as part of the ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא, זֹאת אוֹמֶרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 7 by learning a legal rule from the court's practice
steps.terutzResolutionType: Inference from practice: the court does not judge the money case first because plowing money is not part of the ox
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Plowing earnings could pay the damage, so the court should judge the money case first
steps.terutzMaskana: Plowing earnings are the owner's general property, so they cannot pay this damage. Judging the money case first would gain nothing.

steps.title: Is there an assessment for damages too?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: when judging damages, does the court assess whether the act was strong enough to cause the damage, as it does for killing? Or is the damager liable for any damage at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: Is there an assessment for damages, or not? Do we say we assess only for killing, to see whether this blow could take a life or not, but for damages he pays for any harm at all? Or perhaps there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. It asks whether the court's check, "was this act enough to cause this result?", applies to damages as well as to killing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For killing, the court checks whether the blow was strong enough to kill. If not, the death is blamed on other causes. The question is whether damages work differently, so that the damager pays for any injury no matter how weak the act was, or the same, so that a weak act that could not normally injure would leave him exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: "A question was asked before them": an open question among the חכמים
Assessment: the court checks whether the act was strong enough to cause the result
Damages, injuries to property or body
Anything at all, even the smallest amount

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up whether a damager can escape liability by showing his act was too weak to normally cause the harm.

phrases.english: A question was asked of them:
Is there an assessment for damages,
or is there no assessment for damages?
Do we say: it is for killing that we assess,
whether with this a soul departs,
or with this a soul does not depart;
but for damages, he is liable for anything at all;
or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: יֵשׁ אוֹמֶד לִנְזָקִין, אוֹ אֵין אוֹמֶד לִנְזָקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, linked to the assessment the ברייתא requires for killing
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the court assesses if an act was strong enough to cause damage, as it does for killing, or holds the damager liable for any damage

steps.title: A proof attempt from the pit less than ten טפחים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about pits: a pit deep enough to kill is ten טפחים. If it is shallower and an animal dies, the digger is exempt, but if the animal is only injured, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Just as a pit deep enough to kill is ten handbreadths, so too anything deep enough to kill is ten handbreadths. If they were less than ten handbreadths, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is exempt. If it was injured in it, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to try to answer the question. It sets up a proof that will be worked out in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a pit under ten טפחים cannot kill, so the digger is exempt if the animal dies there. But he is liable for an injury in that same shallow pit, with no mention of checking how deep it must be to injure. This seems to suggest that for damages there is no assessment and any injury makes him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: "Come and hear": the גמרא brings a source to try to answer the question
A pit, one of the main categories of damagers
Ten handbreadths, the depth needed for a pit to kill

steps.confusionAlert: The proof is not finished here. The גמרא will still examine whether this משנה really shows there is no assessment for damages.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה on 50b.

phrases.aramaic: מָה בּוֹר – שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית,
phrases.english: Just as a pit that has enough depth to kill
is ten handbreadths deep;

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית,
phrases.english: so too, anything that has enough depth to kill
phrases.notes: "Anything" here means other dug-out holes, like ditches and caves.

phrases.english: is ten handbreadths deep.
If they were less than ten handbreadths,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר וָמֵת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is exempt.
If it was injured in it, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מָה בּוֹר – שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a משנה to try to settle the question of step 9
steps.raayaObject: Whether there is an assessment for damages
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה on 50b: a pit under ten טפחים is exempt for death but liable for injury

steps.title: Reading the pit משנה as counting upward: no assessment for damages
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the pit משנה as counting from one טפח up to ten. On that reading, a pit of any depth makes the digger liable for injury, so there is no assessment for damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't the משנה counting from the bottom up? It means: from one טפח up to ten, there is no liability for death, but there is liability for damage. So for damage, any depth at all is enough. Learn from this that the court does not assess damages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now draws the conclusion from the pit משנה quoted in step 10. It reads the משנה in a way that would prove there is no assessment for damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even a one-טפח pit makes the digger liable for injuries, the court is not checking whether the pit could really cause the injury. That would mean אין אומדין לנזקין: any damage at all creates liability.

keyTerms.meaning: From below to above (counting up from small to large)
A handbreadth, a unit of measure
Any amount at all, even the smallest
We do not assess whether the act was strong enough to cause the result

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו מִמַּטָּה לְמַעְלָה קָא חָשֵׁיב –
phrases.english: What, is it not counting from below to above
and this is what it is saying:
From one handbreadth until ten
there is no liability for death, but there is liability for damage?
Apparently, for damage, any amount at all is enough
Learn from it: we do not assess for damage!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי, לָאו מִמַּטָּה לְמַעְלָה קָא חָשֵׁיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the pit משנה quoted in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That there is no assessment for damages (אין אומדין לנזקין).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The pit משנה, read as counting from one טפח up to ten.

steps.title: No, the משנה counts downward, so there may still be an assessment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The משנה counts from ten down: a pit of ten kills, and a pit slightly less than ten can injure but not kill. So there may be an assessment for damages after all.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the משנה is counting from the top down. It means: ten טפחים can kill. Slightly less than ten can cause damage but not death. Really, there is an assessment for damages, and in every case we require that the thing be able to cause that damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 11 by reading the משנה the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only teaches about a pit just under ten טפחים, not one that is tiny. A pit that deep can surely injure, so the משנה does not show liability for any depth at all. The question is not settled yet, and the גמרא even suggests that an assessment is needed. Steps 19–20 settle it.

keyTerms.meaning: From above to below (counting down from ten)
Really, I can tell you (keeping the opposite view)

steps.confusionAlert: The משנה's words did not change. Only the direction of counting changed, and that alone flips what the משנה proves.

phrases.english: No, it is counting from above to below
and this is what it is saying:
Ten — there is liability for death
slightly less than ten
there is liability for damage, but not for death.

phrases.aramaic: וּלְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ יֵשׁ אוֹמֶד לִנְזָקִין,
phrases.english: And really, I can tell you there is an assessment for damage
and for each and every thing
we require that it be such that one could be damaged by it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא, מִמַּעְלָה לְמַטָּה קָא חָשֵׁיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 11 by reading the משנה from the top down.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof itself, not the question. It even leaves room for the opposite view.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the משנה counts upward from one טפח. It can just as well count downward from ten.

steps.title: Proof from a slave struck near his eye or ear
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says a slave goes free if his master strikes his eye and blinds him. He does not go free if the master strikes near his eye and he stops seeing. The גמרא suggests the reason is that the blow is assessed, which would prove there is an assessment for damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if a master struck his slave on the eye and blinded him, or on the ear and deafened him, the slave goes free. If he struck near the eye and the slave cannot see, or near the ear and he cannot hear, the slave does not go free. Why? Isn't it because we require an assessment? Learn from this that there is an assessment for damages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof from a ברייתא, this time for the opposite side: that there is an assessment for damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the slave really lost his sight or hearing. The only difference is where the blow landed. If a blow near the eye does not count, it seems the court judges that such a blow could not cause blindness, and that is an assessment.

keyTerms.meaning: Near (facing) his eye, not on it

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If he struck him on his eye and blinded him
phrases.notes: This is a master striking his Canaanite slave.

phrases.english: or on his ear and deafened him
the slave goes free because of these.
If he struck near his eye and he does not see
or near his ear and he does not hear
the slave does not go free because of these.
What is the reason?
Isn't it because we require an assessment?
So learn from it: there is an assessment for damage?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הִכָּהוּ עַל עֵינוֹ וְסִימְּאוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected, a new source is brought, this time for the opposite side.
steps.raayaObject: That there is an assessment for damages (יש אומדנא לנזקין).
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a master striking his slave on or near the eye or ear.

steps.title: No, the slave may have frightened himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The slave does not go free because the injury may have come from his own fright, not from the master's blow.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the reason is that we say he frightened himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 13 by giving a different reason for the ברייתא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the blow lands near the eye, the blindness may have come from the slave's own fright. In that case the master did not directly cause the injury. The ruling has nothing to do with assessing how strong the blow was.

phrases.english: No; it is because we say:
it was he who frightened himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמְרִינַן: הוּא דְּאַבְעֵית נַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 13 by giving another reason for the ruling.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the slave ברייתא. The question is not settled yet; steps 19–20 settle it.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the only possible reason was an assessment. The real reason could be that the slave's own fright caused the injury.

steps.title: Support: one who frightens another is exempt in human court
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that fright can cause injury and that frightening someone is treated differently from physically harming him. Shouting into someone's ear is exempt in human court, but holding him and shouting is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: one who frightens another person is exempt under human law but liable under the laws of Heaven. How so? If he shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is exempt. If he held him and shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support its explanation that a fright injury does not make someone liable in human court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Frightening someone, without physical contact, is not punished by human courts, though Heaven holds the person responsible. Physical contact, like holding the person, changes this and makes him liable. So the slave case can be explained as a fright injury that does not count.
steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs so far were rejected. The pit משנה can be read as counting down from ten, and the slave case can be explained as an injury from fright. The גמרא keeps looking for a source, and steps 19–20 finally prove that there is an assessment for damages.

phrases.english: As it is taught: one who frightens his fellow
is exempt by human law
but liable by the laws of Heaven.
How so?
If he shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is exempt
if he held him and shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְתַנְיָא: הַמַּבְעִית אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection in step 14 by showing that a fright injury is exempt in human court.
steps.raayaObject: That injury caused by fright alone is not liable in human court.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about one who frightens his fellow.

steps.title: Proof from the five payments that are assessed in advance
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the court assesses the injured person ahead of time and pays him right away. The גמרא concludes that there is an assessment for damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: for five kinds of payment, the court assesses the victim and he is paid immediately. Medical costs and lost work are counted until he heals. If they assessed him and he then got worse, he gets only what they assessed. If they assessed him and he got better, he still gets all that they assessed. Learn from this: there is an assessment for damages!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to prove that the court does make an assessment for damages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows the court estimating ahead of time how much the injury will cost. Payment follows that estimate, even if the victim later gets worse or better. Since the court clearly makes an estimate here, the גמרא concludes that there is an assessment for damages.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear; introduces a proof from a source
They assess; the court estimates the amount ahead of time
Payment for work lost while recovering

phrases.english: Come and hear:
For five things, they assess him,
and they give it to him immediately.
Medical costs and lost work: until he heals.
If they assessed him, and he kept getting weaker,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נוֹתְנִין לוֹ אֶלָּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאֲמָדוּהוּ.
phrases.english: they give him only what they assessed him for.
If they assessed him and he got healthy,
they give him all that they assessed him for.
Learn from it: there is an assessment for damages!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: חֲמִשָּׁה דְּבָרִים אוֹמְדִין אוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After earlier proofs were turned away, the גמרא tries a new source.
steps.raayaObject: There is an assessment for damages.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about assessing the five payments in advance and paying right away.

steps.title: Assessing a person was never in question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Assessing how long a person will suffer from an injury is obviously done, and that was never the question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Assessing a man, how long he will suffer from this blow and how long he will not, is not our question, since we certainly assess that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. The ברייתא only shows that we assess a person's injury, and nobody doubted that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is about estimating how long the victim will be hurt. Everyone agrees that kind of estimate is made. So the proof does not touch the real question.

keyTerms.meaning: A man; here, the injured person
He will suffer, be in pain
We have no question about it

phrases.english: To assess a man,
how long he will suffer from this blow
and how long he will not suffer:
we have no question about that,
since we certainly assess it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימַד גַּבְרָא, כַּמָּה לִיקְּצַר מֵיהָא מַכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 16 by narrowing what the question is about.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof is rejected completely, because it proves something nobody doubted.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא is about assessing the victim's recovery, not about assessing the object that caused the injury.

steps.title: The real question: assessing the object
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states its real question: does the court assess an object to see whether it could have caused this injury?
steps.simpleTranslation: Our question is about assessing an object: could it do this damage or not? What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now states its question exactly, which sets up the next proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doubt is whether the court checks the item used, such as a stone or a stick, to see if it could cause this injury. That is what 'assessment for damages' means in this סוגיא.

phrases.english: When we do have a question,
it is about assessing an object:

phrases.aramaic: אִי עָבֵיד הַאי נִזְקָא אוֹ לָא.
phrases.english: whether it can do this damage or not.
What is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָא מִבַּעְיָא לַן – לְמֵימַד חֶפְצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the rejection by stating the true question, then asks for a source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the court assess whether an object was able to cause the injury?

steps.title: Proof from שמעון התימני: the fist is brought before the court
steps.stepSummary: שמעון התימני says a fist, and any similar item, is brought before the judges and witnesses. This shows that objects are assessed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: שמעון התימני says: just as a fist is special in that it is brought before the court and the witnesses, so too anything special that is brought before the court and the witnesses. Learn from this: there is an assessment for damages!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that answers its narrowed question about assessing objects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fist is shown to the judges so they can judge whether it could cause this injury. שמעון התימני applies this to any item that can be checked this way. That is exactly assessing an object, so there is an assessment for damages.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא, from the place תמנה
The assembly of judges, the court

phrases.english: Come and hear: שמעון התימני says:
Just as a fist is special
phrases.notes: The fist comes from the פסוק about a fight, שמות 21:18.

phrases.english: in that it is handed over to the court and to the witnesses,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל מְיוּחָד שֶׁמָּסוּר לָעֵדָה וְלָעֵדִים.
phrases.english: so too, anything special that is handed over to the court and to the witnesses.
Learn from it: there is an assessment for damages!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, שִׁמְעוֹן הַתִּימְנִי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 18.
steps.raayaObject: The court assesses whether an object could cause the injury.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of שמעון התימני comparing any item to a fist that is brought before the court and witnesses.

steps.title: The proof is accepted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the proof: there is an assessment for damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees that the proof works and closes the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time no rejection follows. The סוגיא concludes that the court does assess whether an object could have caused the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it; as a reply, it means the proof is accepted
There is an assessment for damages
An assessment, estimate by the court

steps.whatToRemember: Assessing how long a victim will suffer was never in doubt. The real question was assessing the object, and שמעון התימני proves the court does assess it.
steps.confusionAlert: The same words 'שמע מינה' appear twice in a row. The first ends the proof, and the second, standing alone, is the גמרא saying 'yes, we accept it.'

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the proof in step 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: There is an assessment for damages, including checking whether the object could cause the injury.

steps.title: The early-healing case supports רבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the ruling that a victim who heals early still gets the full amount, and shows that it supports רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: if they assessed him and he got healthy, they give him all that they assessed. This supports רבא, who said: someone who was assessed as unable to work for the whole day, but recovered at midday and was working, gets paid for the whole day. He was owed the whole day; it is from Heaven that they had mercy on him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new point. It quotes a line from the earlier ברייתא again and shows that it supports a ruling of רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא rules that if a victim heals faster than expected, the one who hurt him still pays the full estimate. The ברייתא says the same thing. The early healing is Heaven's kindness to the victim, so it does not lower what the attacker owes.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said; introduces a line quoted earlier in order to discuss it

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule that payment follows the court's assessment, not what actually happens later. That holds whether the victim recovers faster or slower than expected.

phrases.english: The Master said:
If they assessed him and he got healthy,
they give him all that they assessed him for.
This supports רבא,
for רבא said:
Someone whom they assessed for the whole day,
and he recovered at midday
and was doing work,
we give him payment.

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלֵּי יוֹמָא מִן שְׁמַיָּא הוּא (דְּרַחֲמֵי) [דְּרַחִימוּ] עֲלֵיהּ.
phrases.english: He is owed the whole day; it is from Heaven that they had mercy on him.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean 'had mercy.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: אֲמָדוּהוּ וְהִבְרִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא from step 16 to draw a separate lesson from it.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's ruling that a victim who heals early is still paid for the full assessed time.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The line in the ברייתא: 'אמדוהו והבריא נותנין לו כל מה שאמדוהו'.

steps.title: Spit pays only if it hits the body
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of spitting, and רב פפא limits it: the payment applies only when the spit reaches the person himself, not his clothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he spat and the spit reached him, or he pulled off his cloak, and so on. רב פפא said: this was taught only when it reached him, but if it landed on his clothing, there is no payment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting the spitting case from the משנה, and רב פפא narrows it to spit that touches the person's body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה sets a fixed payment for spitting on someone. רב פפא adds a limit: only direct contact with the body counts. Spit that lands only on the clothing does not trigger the payment.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this in the case of...

phrases.english: If he spat and the spit reached him,
or he removed, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' stands for the rest of the משנה: pulling off someone's cloak, and so on, which costs 400 זוז.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בּוֹ,
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: They taught this only when it reached him,
but if it reached his clothing, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב פפא לא שנו אלא בו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new line of the משנה after the discussion of assessments ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The spitting payment applies only when the spit touches the person's body, not his clothing.

steps.title: Shouldn't spit on clothing count like shaming with words?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: even if spit on clothing is not like spit on the body, it should at least be like embarrassing someone with words.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it be like a case where he shamed him with words!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב פפא: spit on someone's clothing is still humiliating, so why not treat it at least like verbal shaming?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumes that shaming someone with words has some payment. If so, spitting on clothing, which is at least as embarrassing, should not be completely free.

phrases.english: Let it be like one who shamed with words!

steps.triggerLanguage: וניהוי כי ביייש בדברים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's exemption for spit on clothing.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that spit on clothing has no payment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Verbal shaming seems to carry some liability, and spit on clothing is at least as bad, so it should not be fully exempt.

steps.title: Shaming with words carries no payment
steps.stepSummary: In the name of רבי יוסי בר אבין, the scholars of ארץ ישראל say that רב פפא's ruling teaches us that shaming someone with words is exempt from any payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the West they say in the name of רבי יוסי בר אבין: this teaches that if he shamed him with words, he is exempt from paying anything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the challenge's assumption is wrong: shaming with words has no payment at all, so comparing to it gains nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed verbal shaming costs money. The answer flips this and learns from רב פפא's ruling itself that words alone carry no court payment. So spit on clothing being free is fully consistent.

keyTerms.meaning: In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

steps.confusionAlert: Being 'exempt' here means the court does not make him pay. It does not mean shaming people with words is allowed.

phrases.english: In the West they say
phrases.notes: 'The West' is ארץ ישראל, which lies west of בבל.

phrases.english: in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin:
That is to say:
phrases.notes: He means that רב פפא's ruling itself proves this point.

phrases.english: if he shamed him with words, he is exempt from anything.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמרי במערבא משמיה דרבי יוסי בר אבין זאת אומרת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 23.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Shaming with words carries some payment, so spit on clothing should too.
steps.terutzMaskana: Shaming with words carries no payment at all, so spit on clothing being exempt makes sense.
steps.whatToRemember: Spit pays only if it touches the body. Shaming with words alone has no court payment.

steps.title: Does 'according to his honor' lower or raise the payment?
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's line 'everything follows his honor,' the גמרא asks whether the תנא קמא means it as a leniency (a poor person gets less than the fixed amounts) or as a stringency (a rich person gets more).
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: everything follows his honor, etc. They asked: does the first תנא say this as a leniency or as a stringency? As a leniency, meaning there is a poor person who doesn't need to receive so much. Or perhaps as a stringency, meaning there is a rich person who must be given more?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line of the משנה and asks which direction it works in: does it make the payment smaller or bigger?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists fixed amounts for each insult, then says 'everything follows his honor.' This could mean a poor person gets less than the listed amounts. Or it could mean a rich person gets more than them.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in the משנה
As a leniency / as a stringency

phrases.english: Everything is according to his honor, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' in square brackets is part of the corrected wording; some versions don't have it.

phrases.english: They asked:
Does the first tanna say this as a leniency,
or does he say it as a stringency?
He says it as a leniency: that there is a poor man
who doesn't need to take this much,
phrases.notes: 'This much' means the fixed amounts the משנה listed.

phrases.english: or perhaps he says it as a stringency:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִיכָּא עָשִׁיר דְּבָעֵי לְמִיתַּב לֵיהּ טְפֵי?
phrases.english: that there is a rich man to whom he must give more?

steps.triggerLanguage: איבעיא להו תנא קמא לקולא קאמר או לחומרא קאמר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'everything follows his honor' reduces the fixed amounts for the poor or increases them for the rich.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא's reply proves it was a leniency
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers that even poor Jews are treated as nobility who lost their wealth. That only makes sense if the תנא קמא had lowered the payment for poor people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: from what רבי עקיבא says, 'Even the poor of Israel are viewed as free men who lost their property, for they are children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב,' learn from this that the first תנא said it as a leniency!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings proof from רבי עקיבא's response in the same משנה to answer the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא is arguing for the poor, saying they deserve the full amounts. That means the תנא קמא must have said a poor person gets less. So 'according to his honor' was a leniency.

keyTerms.meaning: Free men, people of noble standing

phrases.english: Come hear: from what Rabbi Akiva says:
Even the poor of Israel

phrases.aramaic: רוֹאִין אוֹתָן כְּאִילּוּ הֵן בְּנֵי חוֹרִין
phrases.english: are viewed as though they were free men
who lost their property,
for they are the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob;

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ, תַּנָּא קַמָּא לְקוּלָּא קָאָמַר!
phrases.english: learn from it: the first tanna says it as a leniency!

steps.triggerLanguage: תא שמע מדקאמר רבי עקיבא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 25.
steps.raayaObject: That the תנא קמא's 'according to his honor' is a leniency.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי עקיבא's statement in the משנה that even poor Jews are treated as nobility.

steps.title: Accepted: it was a leniency
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the proof: the תנא קמא meant that a poor person may receive less.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from it, yes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees with the proof and closes the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No challenge is raised against the proof. The final reading is that the תנא קמא lowers the payment for a poor person, and רבי עקיבא disagrees.
steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא's 'everything follows his honor' can lower the payment for a poor person. רבי עקיבא holds that every Jew deserves the full amount because they are all children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב.

phrases.english: Learn from it, indeed.

steps.triggerLanguage: שמע מינה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms the proof of Step 26.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The תנא קמא spoke as a leniency: a poor person may receive less than the fixed amounts.

steps.title: How could רבי עקיבא give the man extra time to pay?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's story, where רבי עקיבא let the man pay later. It challenges this with רבי חנינא's rule that the court gives no extra time for injuries.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה tells of a man who uncovered a woman's head, and רבי עקיבא gave him time to pay. But do we give extra time? רבי חנינא said we do not give extra time for injuries!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the story at the end of the משנה. It asks how רבי עקיבא could let the man pay later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the man asked רבי עקיבא for time to pay the 400 זוז, and he got it. רבי חנינא teaches that payments for חבלות must be made right away. So the משנה's story seems to go against a known rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Uncovered the head (took off a woman's hair covering in public)
But do we give...? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: And there was an incident with one who uncovered
the head of a woman, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points to the rest of the משנה's story: the man asked רבי עקיבא for time to pay, and he got it.

phrases.english: But do we give time to pay?
But didn't Rabbi Ḥanina say:
We do not give time to pay for injuries!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי יָהֲבִינַן זְמַן? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the discussion of 'everything follows his honor' to the story at the end of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's giving the man time to pay in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חנינא rules that no extra time is given for injury payments, so the story seems to break that rule.

steps.title: No extra time for injury, but extra time for shame
steps.stepSummary: The 'no extra time' rule applies only to חבלה, which causes a real money loss. For בושת, which causes no money loss, extra time may be given.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we don't give time, that is for injury, because he made the victim lose money. But for shame, where he didn't make him lose money, we do give time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting רבי חנינא's rule to real injury.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A physical injury costs the victim real money right away, for example doctor bills and lost work, so the injurer must pay at once. בושת hurts feelings but does not take money from the victim's pocket. So the court can let him pay later, as רבי עקיבא did.

keyTerms.meaning: He caused him a money loss

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that payments for חבלה and payments for בושת can follow different rules, which sets up the next part of the סוגיא.

phrases.english: When we do not give him time
it is for injury, since he caused him a money loss;
but for shame,
where he did not cause him a money loss, we do give time.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי לָא יָהֲבִינַן לֵיהּ זְמַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבי חנינא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule (חבלה versus בושת)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי חנינא's rule seemed to cover every payment for hurting someone, including בושת.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only חבלה, which causes a money loss, must be paid right away. For בושת, extra time may be given.

steps.title: A ברייתא says רבי עקיבא allowed a person to injure himself
steps.stepSummary: The משנה tells how the man tricked the woman into uncovering her own head, and רבי עקיבא still made him pay. A ברייתא has רבי עקיבא saying a person is allowed to injure himself, which seems to contradict this.
steps.simpleTranslation: He waited for her to stand at the door of her courtyard, etc. But a ברייתא teaches that רבי עקיבא said to him: You dove into mighty waters and came up with only a broken clay piece in your hand, since a person is allowed to injure himself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה's story. It then raises a ברייתא where רבי עקיבא seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the man got the woman to uncover her own head, then claimed she had shamed herself. רבי עקיבא answered that a person may not injure himself, and still made the man pay. In the ברייתא, רבי עקיבא tells the man his clever proof was worth nothing: even though a person is allowed to injure himself, the one who caused the harm still pays. The two sources disagree about whether hurting oneself is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: He watched and waited for her
But a ברייתא teaches... (brings a contradicting source)
You dove into mighty waters (you worked very hard)

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמָרָהּ עוֹמֶדֶת עַל פֶּתַח חֲצֵירָהּ וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: He waited for her until she stood at the door of her courtyard, etc.
phrases.notes: In the משנה he tricked her into uncovering her own hair. רבי עקיבא said a person may not injure himself, and still made him pay.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: Rabbi Akiva said to him:
You dove into mighty waters
and brought up a clay shard in your hand,
phrases.notes: A picture of all that effort for nothing: the man's clever plan doesn't help him.

phrases.english: a person is allowed to injure himself!

steps.confusionAlert: In both sources, רבי עקיבא makes the man pay. The contradiction is only about the reason, whether a person is or is not allowed to hurt himself.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא, אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next detail in the משנה's story.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's statement in the משנה that a person may not injure himself
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא quotes רבי עקיבא saying a person is allowed to injure himself, which directly contradicts the משנה.

steps.title: רבא: one source is about injury, the other about shame
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the two sources speak about different cases. One is about חבלה, real physical injury, and the other is about בושת, shaming oneself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is not difficult. Here it is about injury; there it is about shame.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא settles the contradiction by saying each source is talking about a different kind of self-harm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא says that hurting your body is not allowed, and that is what the משנה means. Shaming yourself is allowed, and that is what the ברייתא means. So רבי עקיבא does not contradict himself.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
Here... there (each source is about a different case)

phrases.english: Rava said: It is not difficult;
here it is about injury, there it is about shame.
phrases.notes: The משנה's 'not allowed' is about physical injury. The ברייתא's 'allowed' is about shaming oneself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to talk about the same kind of self-harm.
steps.terutzMaskana: Self-injury is not allowed. Shaming oneself is allowed.

steps.title: But the משנה itself is about shame
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on רבא: the משנה's case, uncovering one's own hair, is a case of בושת, not physical injury.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה is about shame,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a challenge against רבא's answer. The sentence continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said the משנה was about real injury. But the woman in the משנה only uncovered her hair, which is shame, not a bodily injury. So רבא's split does not seem to fit the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: But surely... (pushes back on what was just said)

phrases.english: But the mishna is about shame,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא מַתְנִיתִין בְּבוֹשֶׁת הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer from step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the משנה is about חבלה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's case of uncovering one's own hair is clearly בושת, so it cannot be the 'injury' side of רבא's split.
